subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: The first law of thermodynamics and its sign convention
Work done when a gas changes volume
Change in internal energy from change in temperature
Entropy as a measure of disorder
The second law in three forms
The adiabatic equation for a monatomic ideal gas

questions.q: Helium in a cylinder fitted with a piston is a closed system. During one process the piston does 600 J of work on the helium, and the helium loses 400 J of thermal energy to its surroundings. Using Clausius' sign convention, what is the change in internal energy ΔU of the helium?
optionWhy: Thermal energy is lost, so Q = −400 J; work is done on the gas, so W = −600 J. Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J. The work done on the gas adds more energy than the heat removes.

A student who substitutes the sizes Q = 400 J and W = 600 J without signs gets ΔU = 400 − 600 = −200 J. The helium LOSES thermal energy (Q = −400 J) and has work done ON it (W = −600 J), so ΔU = −400 − (−600) = +200 J.

A student who takes the work done on the gas as W = +600 J, as in the chemistry form ΔU = Q + W, but uses Q = ΔU + W gets ΔU = −400 − 600 = −1000 J. In Clausius' convention work done on the system is negative, W = −600 J, which gives ΔU = +200 J.

A student who thinks only heating and cooling change internal energy sets ΔU = Q = −400 J. The 600 J of work done by the piston also transfers energy to the helium, so ΔU = Q − W = −400 − (−600) = +200 J.
questions.explain: Thermal energy is lost, so Q = −400 J; work is done on the gas, so W = −600 J. Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J. The work done on the gas adds more energy than the heat removes.
questions.working: Clausius' sign convention: Q is the thermal energy supplied to the helium, so Q = −400 J (energy lost); W is the work done BY the helium, so W = −600 J (work done on it). Q = ΔU + W, so ΔU = Q − W = −400 J − (−600 J) = +200 J = +2.0 × 10² J.

questions.q: A fixed mass of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is taken from state X to state Y. On a P–V diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis) the process is a straight line from X (2.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) to Y (6.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa), where each state is given as (volume, pressure). What is the work W, as it appears in Q = ΔU + W, for this process?
optionWhy: A student who treats W as the work done ON the gas gives the expansion a negative sign. In Clausius' convention W is the work done BY the gas, positive when the gas expands, as it does here.

A student who uses W = PΔV with the final pressure, 3.0 × 10⁵ × 4.0 × 10⁻³ = 1200 J, has treated the pressure as constant. It rises from 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa to 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa, so the work is the trapezium area under the line, 800 J.
The pressure is not constant, so W is the area under the straight-line path, a trapezium: W = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ + 3.0 × 10⁵) Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 800 J. It is positive because the gas expands.
A student who reads PΔV as the change in PV calculates P_YV_Y − P_XV_X = 1800 − 200 = 1600 J. That quantity equals nRΔT, not the work; the work is the area under the path, 800 J.
questions.explain: The pressure is not constant, so W is the area under the straight-line path, a trapezium: W = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ + 3.0 × 10⁵) Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 800 J. It is positive because the gas expands.
questions.working: Pressure varies, so W = area under the P–V path. For a straight line this is a trapezium: W = ½(P_X + P_Y)(V_Y − V_X) = ½(1.0 × 10⁵ Pa + 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) × (6.0 − 2.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 4.0 × 10⁻³ m³ = 8.0 × 10² J. The gas expands, so W = +8.0 × 10² J.

questions.q: Two identical samples, X and Y, each contain the same amount of helium, a monatomic ideal gas, at 300 K. X is heated at constant volume and Y is heated at constant pressure, and both finish at 350 K. Which comparison of the two processes is correct?
options: ΔU is greater for Y, as more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.
Y has the smaller ΔU, since it loses some of its energy as work as it expands.
ΔU is greater for Y, since its atoms move further apart and gain potential energy.
ΔU is the same for both, but more thermal energy must be supplied to Y than to X.
optionWhy: A student who thinks all the thermal energy supplied becomes internal energy picks this. Y does need more heat, but the extra leaves as work done by the expanding gas; ΔU depends only on ΔT, which is the same for X and Y.

A student who thinks ΔU depends on the process picks this. For an ideal gas ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, so equal temperature changes give equal ΔU. The work done by Y is extra energy supplied as heat, not energy taken from its internal energy.

A student who includes intermolecular potential energy in the internal energy of an ideal gas picks this. The ideal gas model has no intermolecular forces, so U is kinetic energy only and depends only on temperature.
ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT depends only on the temperature change, which is the same for both. Y expands and does work W = nRΔT, so it needs Q = ΔU + W, more than X, for which W = 0 and Q = ΔU.
questions.explain: ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT depends only on the temperature change, which is the same for both. Y expands and does work W = nRΔT, so it needs Q = ΔU + W, more than X, for which W = 0 and Q = ΔU.

questions.q: A beaker of crushed ice at 0 °C is left in a warm room. The ice melts completely, and at the moment melting finishes the liquid water is still at 0 °C. Which statement correctly compares the entropy of the sample as liquid water with its entropy as crushed ice?
options: The water has the greater entropy: its molecules are arranged far less regularly than in ice, although the temperature is unchanged.
The crushed ice has the greater entropy: a jumble of fragments is a more disordered arrangement than a smooth body of liquid.
The two are equal: entropy is fixed by the temperature, and the sample is at 0 °C both before and after it melts.
The two are equal: entropy, like energy, is conserved, so the entropy of the ice is carried unchanged into the water.
optionWhy: Entropy relates to the degree of disorder of the particles. In ice the molecules sit in a regular crystal lattice; in liquid water they are free to move past one another and can be arranged in many more ways. The disorder of the particles, and so the entropy, increases on melting even though the temperature stays at 0 °C; thermodynamically, ΔS = ΔQ/T with ΔQ the latent heat absorbed.

A student who reads 'disorder' as visible untidiness picks this. Entropy concerns the arrangement and motion of the particles, not the shape of the lumps. Inside every fragment the water molecules are locked in a regular lattice; in the liquid they are far less ordered, so the water has the greater entropy.

A student who thinks entropy is a measure of temperature picks this. Entropy depends on how the particles are arranged as well as on their energy: at the same temperature the liquid's molecules are far less ordered than the crystal's, so the entropy rises on melting. ΔS = ΔQ/T is non-zero here because latent heat ΔQ is absorbed at constant T.

A student who treats entropy as a conserved quantity picks this. Entropy is not conserved: it is a measure of the disorder of the particles, and it increases when a regular crystal becomes a liquid. The water's entropy exceeds the ice's by the latent heat absorbed divided by 273 K.
questions.explain: Entropy relates to the degree of disorder of the particles. In ice the molecules sit in a regular crystal lattice; in liquid water they are free to move past one another and can be arranged in many more ways. The disorder of the particles, and so the entropy, increases on melting even though the temperature stays at 0 °C; thermodynamically, ΔS = ΔQ/T with ΔQ the latent heat absorbed.

questions.q: Four identical fair coins are tossed. Each particular sequence of heads (H) and tails (T), such as HTHT, is a microstate, and all microstates are equally probable. The macrostate is the total number of heads. What is the probability of the macrostate 'two heads'?
optionWhy: A student who assumes the five macrostates (0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 heads) are equally likely gets 1/5. It is the 16 microstates that are equally probable; 'two heads' has 6 of them, 'four heads' only 1.
A student who counts 'two heads' as the single arrangement HHTT gets 1/16. Six different sequences contain exactly two heads, so the probability is 6/16.
There are 2⁴ = 16 equally probable microstates. Six of them have exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH and TTHH. P = 6/16 = 37.5%.

A student who confuses the fraction of coins showing heads (2 of 4) with the probability of the outcome gets 1/2. The probability is the number of microstates in the macrostate divided by the total: 6/16.
questions.explain: There are 2⁴ = 16 equally probable microstates. Six of them have exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH and TTHH. P = 6/16 = 37.5%.
questions.working: Total microstates = 2⁴ = 16, all equally probable. Microstates with exactly two heads: HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, so Ω = 6. P = 6/16 = 0.375 = 37.5%.

questions.q: A set of four fair coins changes from the macrostate 'four heads' to the macrostate 'two heads'. Using S = k_B ln Ω, where Ω is the number of microstates of the macrostate and k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, what is the change in entropy, expressed as a multiple of k_B and in J K⁻¹?
optionWhy: A student who leaves out the logarithm calculates ΔS = k_B × 6 − k_B × 1 = 5k_B = 6.90 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. Entropy is S = k_B ln Ω, so ΔS = k_B ln 6 − k_B ln 1 = k_B ln 6.
A student who presses the base-10 log key gets k_B log₁₀ 6 = 0.78k_B = 1.07 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The formula uses the natural logarithm: ln 6 = 1.79, not 0.778.

A student who uses Ω = 16, the total number of microstates of four coins, for the 'two heads' macrostate gets k_B ln 16 = 2.77k_B. Ω counts only the microstates of the macrostate in question: six for 'two heads'.
'Four heads' has one microstate (Ω = 1, S = 0); 'two heads' has six. ΔS = k_B ln 6 − k_B ln 1 = 1.79k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 1.79 = 2.47 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
questions.explain: 'Four heads' has one microstate (Ω = 1, S = 0); 'two heads' has six. ΔS = k_B ln 6 − k_B ln 1 = 1.79k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 1.79 = 2.47 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
questions.working: Microstates: 'four heads' → HHHH only, Ω₁ = 1; 'two heads' → HHTT, HTHT, HTTH, THHT, THTH, TTHH, Ω₂ = 6. ΔS = k_B ln Ω₂ − k_B ln Ω₁ = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × (ln 6 − ln 1) = 1.792k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 1.792 = 2.47 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. (check.key evaluates the multiple of k_B, 1.79.)

questions.q: An inventor claims to have built a device that, operating in a cycle, extracts 1000 J of thermal energy from seawater at 290 K in each cycle and delivers 1000 J of work, with no other effect. Which judgement of this claim is correct?
options: Impossible: although it conserves energy, it breaks the Kelvin form of the second law.
Possible: the work output equals the thermal energy input, so no law of physics is broken.
Impossible: seawater at 290 K is cold, so it contains no thermal energy to extract.
Possible, but only if all friction and heat leaks in the device are removed.
optionWhy: The Kelvin form says no device operating in a cycle can extract thermal energy from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work. Energy is conserved here, so the first law is satisfied, but the second law forbids the device.

A student who thinks energy conservation is the only constraint picks this. The first law is satisfied, but the second law (Kelvin form) forbids any cyclic device that turns heat from one reservoir entirely into work.
A student who thinks cold bodies contain no heat picks this. Seawater at 290 K has a very large internal energy. The claim fails because of the second law, not because the energy is absent.

A student who thinks friction is the only cause of inefficiency picks this. Even a frictionless device must reject some thermal energy to a colder reservoir; complete conversion from one reservoir is forbidden by the Kelvin form.
questions.explain: The Kelvin form says no device operating in a cycle can extract thermal energy from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work. Energy is conserved here, so the first law is satisfied, but the second law forbids the device.

questions.q: A rigid, insulated container is divided by a partition. One half contains helium, a monatomic ideal gas; the other half is a vacuum. The partition is removed and the gas spreads freely through the whole container, which forms an isolated system. What happens to the entropy of the gas?
options: It is unchanged, because no heat is transferred and so ΔS = ΔQ/T = 0.
It decreases, as the expanding gas does work and cools, so its entropy falls.
It increases, as the free expansion is irreversible although Q = 0.
It is unchanged, since entropy, like energy, is conserved in an isolated system.
optionWhy: A student who applies ΔS = ΔQ/T to every process picks this. That relation holds for reversible transfers. The free expansion is irreversible, and the entropy increases because the gas has more microstates in the larger volume.

A student who thinks a gas does work whenever it expands picks this. Expanding into a vacuum, the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0; with Q = 0 as well, ΔU = 0 and the temperature of the ideal gas is unchanged.

The gas spreads into twice the volume, so many more microstates are available to it and S = k_B ln Ω increases. The expansion is irreversible: the gas does not return to one half by itself. ΔS = ΔQ/T does not apply to an irreversible process.

A student who thinks entropy is conserved like energy picks this. Energy is conserved in the isolated container, but entropy increases in every irreversible process, and free expansion is irreversible.
questions.explain: The gas spreads into twice the volume, so many more microstates are available to it and S = k_B ln Ω increases. The expansion is irreversible: the gas does not return to one half by itself. ΔS = ΔQ/T does not apply to an irreversible process.
questions.working: Isolated, so Q = 0; the gas pushes on nothing, so W = 0; hence ΔU = 0 and the temperature of the ideal gas is unchanged. The volume available to each atom doubles, so the number of microstates Ω increases and S = k_B ln Ω increases. The expansion is irreversible (the gas never returns to one half by itself), so ΔS > 0 even though Q = 0; ΔS = ΔQ/T applies only to reversible transfers.

questions.q: In one minute a refrigerator removes 3000 J of thermal energy from its interior, which stays at 250 K, and delivers 4000 J of thermal energy to the kitchen, which stays at 300 K. What is the total entropy change of the interior and the kitchen in that minute?
options: −12 J K⁻¹; the work done lets the total entropy decrease
0 J K⁻¹; all the entropy that leaves the interior reaches the kitchen
+25 J K⁻¹; the interior and the kitchen both gain entropy
+1.3 J K⁻¹; the kitchen gains more entropy than the interior loses
optionWhy: A student who counts only the interior and thinks work overrides the second law gets −12 J K⁻¹. The 4000 J delivered to the kitchen raises its entropy by 13.3 J K⁻¹, so the total increases.

A student who thinks entropy is conserved assumes the kitchen gains exactly the 12 J K⁻¹ the interior loses. The kitchen receives 4000 J at 300 K, which is 13.3 J K⁻¹, so the total rises by 1.3 J K⁻¹.
A student who thinks every part gains entropy adds 12.0 and 13.3 J K⁻¹. The interior loses thermal energy, so its entropy decreases by 12.0 J K⁻¹; the total is 13.3 − 12.0 = +1.3 J K⁻¹.

Interior: ΔS = −3000/250 = −12.0 J K⁻¹. Kitchen: ΔS = +4000/300 = +13.3 J K⁻¹. Total = +1.3 J K⁻¹. The interior's entropy decreases locally, but the kitchen's increases by more, as the second law requires.
questions.explain: Interior: ΔS = −3000/250 = −12.0 J K⁻¹. Kitchen: ΔS = +4000/300 = +13.3 J K⁻¹. Total = +1.3 J K⁻¹. The interior's entropy decreases locally, but the kitchen's increases by more, as the second law requires.
questions.working: Interior: ΔS = ΔQ/T = −3000 J ÷ 250 K = −12.0 J K⁻¹. Kitchen: ΔS = +4000 J ÷ 300 K = +13.3 J K⁻¹. Total ΔS = −12.0 + 13.3 = +1.3 J K⁻¹ (positive, consistent with the second law).

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is compressed adiabatically. The piston does 450 J of work on the gas. Which statement correctly describes the change?
options: ΔU = +450 J and T rises, as Q = 0 and W = −450 J
ΔU = 0 and T is unchanged, as no heat enters the gas
ΔU = −450 J and T falls, because Q = 0 and W = +450 J
ΔU = +450 J but T is unchanged; the energy is stored as PE
optionWhy: Adiabatic means Q = 0. Work is done on the gas, so W = −450 J. Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = +450 J, and since ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, the temperature rises.
A student who thinks adiabatic means constant temperature picks this. No heat enters, but 450 J of work is done on the gas, which raises its internal energy and hence its temperature.
A student who takes work done on the gas as positive W gets ΔU = Q − W = −450 J. In Clausius' convention work done on the system is negative, so ΔU = +450 J.

A student who thinks an ideal gas stores intermolecular potential energy picks this. An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so its internal energy is kinetic only and an increase in U means an increase in T.
questions.explain: Adiabatic means Q = 0. Work is done on the gas, so W = −450 J. Q = ΔU + W gives ΔU = +450 J, and since ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, the temperature rises.
questions.working: Adiabatic: Q = 0. Work done on the gas: W = −450 J. Q = ΔU + W → 0 = ΔU − 450 J → ΔU = +450 J. For a monatomic ideal gas ΔU = (3/2)nRΔT, so ΔT > 0: the temperature rises.

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, at 27 °C is compressed adiabatically to one-eighth of its initial volume. For this process PV^(5/3) = constant. What is the final temperature of the helium?
optionWhy: A student who thinks adiabatic means constant temperature keeps T = 300 K. No heat is transferred, but the work done on the gas raises its internal energy, so its temperature rises to 1200 K.
PV^(5/3) = constant gives P₂/P₁ = 8^(5/3) = 32. Then PV/T = constant gives T₂ = T₁ × (P₂/P₁) × (V₂/V₁) = 300 K × 32 × (1/8) = 1200 K.
A student who multiplies the temperature by the pressure ratio, 32, has used P ∝ T, which holds only at constant volume. The volume falls by a factor of 8, so T₂ = 300 × 32 ÷ 8 = 1200 K.
A student who uses 27, the temperature in °C, gets 27 × 4 = 108 °C = 381 K. The gas laws need absolute temperature: T₁ = 300 K, so T₂ = 1200 K.
questions.explain: PV^(5/3) = constant gives P₂/P₁ = 8^(5/3) = 32. Then PV/T = constant gives T₂ = T₁ × (P₂/P₁) × (V₂/V₁) = 300 K × 32 × (1/8) = 1200 K.
questions.working: Initial T₁ = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Adiabatic: P₁V₁^(5/3) = P₂V₂^(5/3), so P₂/P₁ = (V₁/V₂)^(5/3) = 8^(5/3) = 32. Ideal gas: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, so T₂ = T₁ × (P₂/P₁)(V₂/V₁) = 300 K × 32 × 1/8 = 1200 K = 1.2 × 10³ K. (Equivalently T₂ = T₁(V₁/V₂)^(2/3) = 300 × 4.)

questions.q: Helium, a monatomic ideal gas, is the working substance of an engine. On a P–V diagram (pressure on the vertical axis, volume on the horizontal axis) each cycle is a rectangle with corners A (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), B (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa), C (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) and D (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa), each given as (volume, pressure). The gas goes round the cycle A → B → C → D → A. What is the net work W done by the gas in one cycle?
optionWhy: A → B and C → D are at constant volume, so W = 0. B → C: W = 3.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = +600 J. D → A: W = 1.0 × 10⁵ × (−2.0 × 10⁻³) = −200 J. Net W = +400 J, the area enclosed by the rectangle.
A student who counts only the expansion B → C gets 600 J. Work of 200 J is done on the gas during the compression D → A, so the net work done by the gas is 600 − 200 = 400 J.
A student who adds the sizes of the work in each stage, 600 + 200 J, has ignored signs. Work done on the gas during compression is negative, W = −200 J, so the net work is +400 J.

A student who takes W as the work done on the gas gives the net work a negative sign. The cycle runs clockwise on the P–V diagram, so the gas does net positive work: W = +400 J in Clausius' convention.
questions.explain: A → B and C → D are at constant volume, so W = 0. B → C: W = 3.0 × 10⁵ × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = +600 J. D → A: W = 1.0 × 10⁵ × (−2.0 × 10⁻³) = −200 J. Net W = +400 J, the area enclosed by the rectangle.
questions.working: A → B: V constant, W = 0. B → C: W = PΔV = 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (3.0 − 1.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = +600 J. C → D: V constant, W = 0. D → A: W = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa × (1.0 − 3.0) × 10⁻³ m³ = −200 J. Net W = +600 − 200 = +4.0 × 10² J (= enclosed area ΔP × ΔV = 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa × 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³).

questions.q: An engine takes helium, a monatomic ideal gas, round a rectangular cycle on a P–V diagram, with states given as (volume, pressure): A (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → B (1.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → C (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 3.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → D (3.0 × 10⁻³ m³, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa) → A. The net work done by the gas per cycle is 400 J. Thermal energy is supplied to the gas only during A → B and B → C. What is the efficiency of the engine?
optionWhy: A student who takes the heat supplied during B → C to be only ΔU = (3/2)PΔV = 900 J gets an input of 1200 J. During B → C the gas also does 600 J of work, so Q = 1500 J, the input is 1800 J and η = 22%.

A student who uses 1 − T_c/T_h with the lowest and highest temperatures of the cycle (T ∝ PV, a ratio of 9) gets 89%. That would be the Carnot limit between those temperatures; this cycle's efficiency is W/Q_in = 400/1800 = 22%.
A student who divides the work by the heat rejected during C → D and D → A (900 + 500 = 1400 J) gets 29%. Efficiency divides by the energy supplied, 1800 J.
questions.working: Using ΔU = (3/2)Δ(PV) and W = PΔV. A → B (isovolumetric): W = 0, Q_AB = (3/2)V(P_B − P_A) = 1.5 × 1.0 × 10⁻³ m³ × 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa = 300 J. B → C (isobaric): ΔU = (3/2)PΔV = 900 J, W = PΔV = 600 J, Q_BC = 1500 J. Input Q_h = 300 + 1500 = 1800 J. (Rejected: C → D 900 J, D → A 500 J; 1800 − 1400 = 400 J = W.) η = W/Q_h = 400 ÷ 1800 = 0.22 = 22%.

questions.q: An engineer claims that an engine working between reservoirs at 327 °C and 27 °C does 700 J of work for every 1200 J of thermal energy it absorbs from the hot reservoir. Which evaluation of the claim is correct?
options: Possible: 58% is less than 100%, and the 500 J rejected balances the energy.
Possible: the Carnot limit applies only to engines that run a Carnot cycle.
Possible: 58% is below the Carnot limit of 92% for these two reservoirs.
Impossible: 58% is more than the Carnot limit of 50% for these two reservoirs.
optionWhy: A student who thinks energy conservation is the only limit picks this. The first law is satisfied, but the second law limits any engine between these reservoirs to 1 − 300/600 = 50%.
A student who thinks the Carnot limit belongs to one particular cycle picks this. It applies to every engine working between the two reservoirs, whatever its cycle.
A student who uses the Celsius temperatures gets 1 − 27/327 = 92%. With kelvin temperatures, 1 − 300/600 = 50%, which the claimed 58% exceeds.
The claimed efficiency is 700/1200 = 58%. With T_h = 600 K and T_c = 300 K, η_Carnot = 1 − 300/600 = 50%. No engine between these reservoirs can exceed that, so the claim violates the second law.
questions.explain: The claimed efficiency is 700/1200 = 58%. With T_h = 600 K and T_c = 300 K, η_Carnot = 1 − 300/600 = 50%. No engine between these reservoirs can exceed that, so the claim violates the second law.
